title: Ang 435–461: Asa chhants
tomorrow: what could be darker than a night with a hundred moons?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letters: an education measured by the account you can give. Today the pages turn from letters to love songs.

Every family wedding has its songs: the ones the aunties sing late at night, the ones the whole room knows the chorus to. On ang 435 the Granth turns to songs that sound like that: the chhants of Raag Asa. A bride. A beloved. Youth, waiting, a house to come home to. They are wedding songs, and the beloved in them is the One.
screen: `THE SONGS EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `A BRIDE, A BELOVED.` → `THE BELOVED IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: A chhant is a song form, and Guru Nanak's chhant on ang 436 rings each line out on a long word at the end, raam, almost like a held note. It opens, in paraphrase: young bride, in the bloom of youth, my Beloved is full of joy. The soul is the bride. The One is the groom. All the longing of a wedding, the waiting, the getting ready, the moment of meeting, becomes a picture of the soul and the One. That's why the Granth sounds so at home at a Sikh wedding. The Lavan, the four rounds from last week, use the same picture: the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib, and the hymns sing of two people and of the soul and the One, at once. And in these songs, every listener is the bride. Married or not, any age, a man or a woman. The union they sing about is open to everyone in the room, including the guest from another faith sitting on the floor near the back.
screen: `CHHANTS: SONGS OF UNION.` · `THE SOUL IS THE BRIDE.` · `THE SAME PICTURE AS THE LAVAN.` · `EVERY LISTENER IS THE BRIDE.` · then, large: `SONGS OF UNION.`

segments.voice: If you can, listen to a recording of a chhant from Raag Asa, or read the one on ang 436 aloud, letting the last word of each line ring out. Then hum one long, low note as you breathe out, and let it fade. Do that a few times, slowly, and notice where the sound sits in your chest.
Ang 435. The page where the chhants of Raag Asa begin: songs of union, sung to the One.
Your line: songs of union, where every listener, from the front row to the back, is the bride. Till next time.

howItsDone: The Asa chhants are read in order and sung as kirtan, and bridal hymns like them are sung at Sikh weddings alongside the four Lavan; guests of any background are welcome to sit with the sangat, heads covered, and share the langar.
